title: Qi Stagnation
background: Qi stagnation (氣滯) is one of the most fundamental TCM pathological patterns, often linked to emotional stress and the Liver's role in ensuring the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body.
key_concepts: Qi as the fundamental moving/functional energy in TCM physiology
the Liver's role in maintaining free coursing (疏泄) of Qi
how emotional stress can lead to Qi stagnation
typical presentations: distending pain, mood swings, sighing
discussion_questions: What does it mean for Qi to 'stagnate', and how is this different from Qi deficiency?
Why is the Liver specifically associated with Qi stagnation in TCM theory?
Can you give an example of a symptom pattern caused by Qi stagnation?
challenge_questions: How would you explain Qi stagnation to a Western-trained physician who is skeptical of energy-based concepts?
Is there a Western physiological correlate you could use to make Qi stagnation more relatable?
learning_objectives: explain Qi stagnation and its typical clinical presentation in English
connect emotional/psychological stress to TCM pattern theory
practice comparing TCM and Western explanatory frameworks
possible_followups: ask the student to compare Qi stagnation with Blood stasis
ask the student how they would treat a Qi stagnation pattern (acupuncture points, herbs)

title: Yin Deficiency
background: Yin deficiency (陰虛) describes a state where the body's cooling, moistening, and nourishing substances are insufficient, often leading to signs of heat and dryness.
key_concepts: Yin as the material, cooling, moistening aspect of the body
how Yin deficiency generates 'deficiency heat' (虛熱)
common signs: night sweats, malar flush, dry mouth, insomnia
the relationship between Yin deficiency and aging or chronic illness
discussion_questions: How does Yin deficiency differ from excess heat patterns?
Why do Yin deficiency patients often present with symptoms worse in the afternoon or evening?
What organs are most commonly associated with Yin deficiency?
challenge_questions: How would you differentiate Yin deficiency from a Western diagnosis like menopause or hyperthyroidism using only symptom description?
What is the risk of mistakenly treating a Yin deficiency patient with warming herbs?
learning_objectives: describe Yin deficiency and its characteristic signs in English
distinguish deficiency heat from excess heat patterns
practice comparing a TCM pattern with overlapping Western diagnoses
possible_followups: ask the student how lifestyle or diet could aggravate Yin deficiency
ask the student to suggest a treatment principle (e.g., nourish Yin, clear deficiency heat)

title: TCM Pattern Identification vs. Western Diagnosis
background: TCM pattern differentiation (辨證) and Western biomedical diagnosis operate on different logics — one organizes signs and symptoms into a functional pattern, the other identifies a specific disease entity, often via lab tests or imaging.
key_concepts: pattern differentiation (辨證論治) as a holistic, symptom-based reasoning process
the same Western diagnosis can map to multiple different TCM patterns (辨病與辨證的差異)
the same TCM pattern can appear across different Western diagnoses
implications for individualized treatment in TCM vs standardized treatment in biomedicine
TCM_terms: same disease, different treatment (同病異治)
different disease, same treatment (異病同治)
discussion_questions: Can you give an example where two patients with the same Western diagnosis would receive different TCM treatments?
What are the strengths and limitations of pattern-based reasoning compared to diagnosis-based reasoning?
How might TCM pattern differentiation and Western diagnosis be used together in an integrative setting?
challenge_questions: A Western physician says TCM pattern differentiation is 'unscientific' because it isn't standardized across patients — how would you respond?
How would you design a study to evaluate the clinical validity of TCM pattern differentiation?
learning_objectives: explain the concept of 'same disease, different treatment' and vice versa
critically compare TCM and Western diagnostic reasoning in English
practice defending TCM methodology using academic, evidence-aware language
possible_followups: push the student to give a concrete clinical example, not just theory
ask the student to propose how integrative medicine clinics could combine both approaches

title: Explaining Acupuncture to a Western Audience
background: Acupuncture is one of the most internationally recognized TCM therapies, but explaining its mechanism to a Western-trained audience requires bridging traditional theory (meridians, Qi) with modern research (neurophysiology, pain gate theory).
key_concepts: meridian theory (經絡) as the traditional explanatory framework
modern research on acupuncture: endorphin release, gate control theory of pain
common conditions acupuncture is used for (pain, nausea, some functional disorders)
the difference between traditional and 'medical acupuncture' framing
discussion_questions: How would you explain what 'Qi' means when describing acupuncture to someone unfamiliar with TCM?
What modern scientific explanations exist for how acupuncture may relieve pain?
What conditions have the strongest evidence base for acupuncture treatment?
challenge_questions: A skeptical colleague says acupuncture is 'just placebo' — how would you respond using both TCM theory and research evidence?
How would you explain the concept of De Qi sensation to a patient who has never had acupuncture?
learning_objectives: explain acupuncture's traditional and modern rationale in accessible English
practice addressing skepticism professionally and evidence-based
build vocabulary for describing acupuncture technique and sensation
possible_followups: ask the student to describe a specific acupoint and its indication
ask the student how they would explain acupuncture safety to a nervous first-time patient

title: Evidence-Based Discussion of Integrative Medicine
background: Integrative medicine combines TCM and biomedicine in clinical practice. This raises questions about evidence standards, safety (e.g., herb-drug interactions), and how practitioners from both traditions can collaborate.
key_concepts: definition and goals of integrative medicine
evidence hierarchy and how TCM research is evaluated (RCTs, systematic reviews)
herb-drug interaction risk as a key safety concern
models of collaboration between TCM and Western physicians
discussion_questions: What are the main challenges in designing rigorous clinical trials for TCM herbal formulas?
Can you give an example of a known herb-drug interaction that a practitioner should be aware of?
What would an ideal integrative medicine clinic workflow look like?
challenge_questions: A hospital administrator asks you to justify why TCM services should be covered in an integrative program with limited evidence for some conditions — how do you respond?
How should a TCM practitioner handle a patient who doesn't want to disclose their Western medications?
learning_objectives: discuss the evidence landscape of TCM research critically in English
explain herb-drug interaction risk to a professional audience
possible_followups: ask the student for a specific example of TCM research they know of
push the student to address the safety angle, not just the philosophical angle
